projectile-motion.title: Projectile Motion Quiz
projectile-motion.description: Test your understanding of trajectories, range, and time of flight

questions.question: A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff with an initial velocity of 10 m/s. What is the horizontal acceleration of the ball during its flight? (Ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: In projectile motion with no air resistance, there is no horizontal acceleration. The only acceleration is gravity (9.8 m/s²) acting vertically downward. The horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

questions.question: At what launch angle will a projectile achieve maximum range on level ground?
questions.explanation: A projectile launched at 45° achieves maximum range on level ground. This is because sin(2θ) in the range equation R = (v₀²sin(2θ))/g reaches its maximum value of 1 when θ = 45°.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at an angle above the horizontal. At the highest point of its trajectory, which statement is true?
options: Both horizontal and vertical velocities are zero
The vertical velocity is zero, but horizontal velocity is not
The horizontal velocity is zero, but vertical velocity is not
Both velocities are at their maximum
questions.explanation: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, the vertical velocity becomes zero (the projectile momentarily stops rising before falling). However, the horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight, as there is no horizontal acceleration.

questions.question: Two projectiles are launched with the same initial speed. One is launched at 30° and the other at 60°. How do their ranges compare?
questions.explanation: Launch angles that are complementary (add up to 90°) produce the same range. Since 30° + 60° = 90°, both projectiles will have the same range. This is because sin(60°) = sin(120°) and sin(2×30°) = sin(60°) = sin(2×60°) = sin(120°).

questions.question: If you double the initial velocity of a projectile (keeping the angle constant), how does the maximum height change?
questions.explanation: Maximum height H = (v₀²sin²(θ))/(2g). Since H is proportional to v₀², doubling the initial velocity quadruples the maximum height.

questions.question: A soccer ball is kicked at ground level with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at 30° above horizontal. What is its vertical component of velocity? (sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: The vertical component of velocity is v₀sin(θ) = 20 × sin(30°) = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true about projectile motion (ignoring air resistance)?
questions.explanation: The total velocity does NOT remain constant in projectile motion. While horizontal velocity stays constant and vertical acceleration is constant, the vertical velocity changes continuously due to gravity, which changes the magnitude of total velocity.

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally from a 20m high cliff. If it takes 2 seconds to hit the ground, what was its initial horizontal velocity? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: We cannot determine the horizontal velocity from the given information. The time to fall depends only on the height and gravity (vertical motion), not on horizontal velocity. We would need to know the horizontal distance traveled to calculate the horizontal velocity.

questions.question: For a projectile launched at 45° with initial speed v₀, what fraction of the maximum height is reached at half the range?
questions.explanation: At 45° launch angle, the trajectory is symmetric. The maximum height occurs at exactly half the range, so at half the range, the projectile is at its maximum height. Therefore, the fraction is 1 (or 100%).

questions.question: Two projectiles are launched simultaneously from the same point. One is launched horizontally at 10 m/s, the other straight upward at 10 m/s. Which statement is true?
options: They hit the ground at the same time
They reach the same maximum height
questions.explanation: The horizontally launched projectile starts falling immediately, while the upward-launched one must first decelerate, stop, then fall. The horizontal projectile has less vertical distance to cover from its starting point and begins descending immediately, so it hits the ground first.

simple-pendulum.title: Simple Pendulum Quiz
simple-pendulum.description: Test your understanding of periodic motion and pendulum dynamics

questions.question: What is the period of a simple pendulum with length 1m on Earth? (g ≈ 10 m/s², π ≈ 3.14)
If you quadruple the length of a pendulum, how does the period change?
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), the period is proportional to √L. If L becomes 4L, then T becomes √4 × T = 2T. The period doubles.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect the period of a simple pendulum?
questions.explanation: From the formula T = 2π√(L/g) we see that the mass does not play a role in the period length so the answer is mass.

questions.question: What happens to the period of a pendulum if you take it to the Moon (where g is about 1/6 of Earth's gravity)?
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), if g becomes g/6, then T becomes √6 times larger. T_moon = 2π√(L/(g/6)) = √6 × 2π√(L/g) ≈ 2.45 × T_earth.

questions.question: For a simple pendulum, the small angle approximation assumes that that sin(θ) ≈ θ. This approximation works well til approximately:
questions.explanation: The small angle approximation works well till about 15 degrees then the margin of error becomes too big and the formula doesn't work anymore.

questions.question: A pendulum swings back and forth, completing 20 oscillations in 40 seconds. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency f = number of oscillations / time = 20 / 40s. So the answer is 0.5Hz.

questions.question: At the maximum displacement (amplitude) of a pendulum's swing, which of these is correct?
options: Velocity is maximum, acceleration is zero
Velocity is zero, acceleration is maximum
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Both velocity and acceleration are maximum
questions.explanation: At maximum displacement, the pendulum momentarily stops (velocity = 0) before changing direction. At this point, the restoring force and therefore acceleration are at their maximum values, pulling the bob back toward equilibrium.

questions.question: If you double the mass of a pendulum bob while keeping length constant, what happens to the maximum speed of the bob during its swing?
questions.explanation: For the same amplitude, the maximum speed remains the same. From energy conservation: v_max = √(2gh), which depends only on the height difference (amplitude), not on mass. The period also doesn't change with mass.

questions.question: A grandfather clock uses a pendulum to keep time. If the clock runs slow, what adjustment should be made?
options: Increase the mass of the bob
Decrease the mass of the bob
questions.explanation: If the clock runs slow, the period is too long (T = 2π√(L/g)). To decrease the period, you must decrease the length L. Making the pendulum shorter will increase its frequency and make the clock run faster.

inclined-plane.title: Inclined Plane Quiz
inclined-plane.description: Test your understanding of forces, friction, and motion on slopes

questions.question: A block rests on a frictionless inclined plane at 30°. What is the acceleration of the block down the plane? (g = 10 m/s², sim 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: On a frictionless incline, a = g sin(θ) = 10 × sin(30°) = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s². The accelereation depends only on the angle and gravity when there's no friction.

questions.question: A 10 kg block sits on an incline at 30°. What is the component of the weight parallel to the incline? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: The parallel component is F∥ = mg sin(θ) = 10 kg × 10 m/s² × sin(30°) = 100 × 0.5 = 50 N. This is the component that pulls the block down the slope.

questions.question: Which statement is true about the normal force on an inclined plane?
options: It equals the weight of the object
It is always less than the weight
It is perpendicular to the incline surface
It increases as the angle decreases
questions.explanation: The normal force is always perpendicular to the surface of contact. On an incline, N = mg cos(θ), which is less than the full weight mg. As angle increases, normal force decreases.

questions.question: A block is on a 45° incline and has a coefficient of static friction μ = 0.5. Will the block slide?
options: Cannot determine without knowing the normal force
questions.explanation: The block slides if tan(θ) > μ. Since tan(45°) = 1 and μ = 0.5. The block will slide.

questions.question: What happens to normal force as the angle of an inclined plane increases from 0° to 90°
questions.explanation: Normal force N = mg cos(θ). At θ = 0° (horizontal), cos(0°) = 1, so N = mg. At θ = 90° (vertical), cos(90°) = 0, so N = 0. The normal force decreases from mg to 0.

questions.question: A box slides down a 30° incline with kinetic friction coefficient μ = 0.2. What is its acceleration? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866)
questions.explanation: With friction: a = g(sin(θ) - μ cos(θ)) = 10(0.5 - 0.2 × 0.866) = 10(0.5 - 0.173) = 10(0.327) = 3.27 m/s². Friction opposes motion, reducing acceleration.

questions.question: Two identical blocks are placed on inclines of diffrerent angles. Which experiences a greater normal force?
options: The block with a steeper incline
The block on the less steep incline
Both experience the same normal force
Depends on the material of the block
questions.explanation: Since N = mg cos(θ), and cosine decreases as angle increases, the block on the less steep incline will a greater normal force. Material doesn't effect this relationship.

questions.question: At what angle will a block just begin to slide if the coefficient of static friction is 0.577? (tan⁻¹(0.577) ≈ 30°)
questions.explanation: A block just begins to slide when tan(θ) = μ. If μ = 0.577, then θ = tan⁻¹(0.577) = 30°. At angles greater than 30°, the block will slide; at smaller angles, it remains stationary.

questions.question: A block slides from rest down a frictionless 4-meter long incline at 30°. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.explanation: Using energy: mgh = ½mv², where h = L sin(θ) = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m. So v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 2) = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s. Alternatively, use kinematics with a = 5 m/s².

questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect the acceleration of a block sliding down a frictionless incline?
questions.explanation: Since a = g sin(θ), acceleration depends only on g and θ. Mass cancels out in the equation (F = ma becomes mg sin(θ) = ma, so a = g sin(θ)). Length affects time but not acceleration.

spring-mass-system.title: Spring-Mass System Quiz
spring-mass-system.description: Test your understanding of harmonic motion, Hooke's law, and oscillations

questions.question: A spring with spring constant k = 100 N/m is compressed by 0.2m. What is the restoring force?
questions.explanation: Using Hooke's law F = kx = 100 N/m × 0.2 m = 20 N. The negative sign in F = -kx indicates the force opposes the displacement, but the magnitude is 20 N.

questions.question: If you quadruple the mass attached to a spring while keeping the spring constant the same, how does the period change?
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(m/k), the period is proportional to √m. If m becomes 4m, then the period doubles

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT effect the period of a spring-mass system?
questions.explanation: From T = 2π√(m/k), we see that period depends only on mass and spring constant. The amplitude does not affect the period in simple harmonic motion.

questions.question: At what point in its oscillations does a spring-mass system have maximum kinetic energy?
options: At any point, kinetic energy is constant
questions.explanation: At the equilibrium position (x = 0), all energy is kinetic since potential energy is zero. The mass moves fastest through equilibrium, so kinetic energy is maximum. At maximum displacement, the mass momentarily stops (KE = 0).

questions.question: If you double both mass and the spring constant, what happens to the period?
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(m/k). If both m and k are doubled: T_new = 2π√(2m/2k) = 2π√(m/k) = T. The period stays the same because the ratio m/k remains unchanged.

questions.question: A spring-mass system oscillates with amplitude A. At what displacement from equilibrium is the speed equal to half the maximum speed?
questions.explanation: Using energy conservation: ½kA² = ½kx² + ½mv². When v = v_max/2, solving gives x = A√3/2 ≈ 0.866A. At this position, the kinetic energy is 1/4 of maximum kinetic energy.

questions.question: What is the total mechanical energy of a spring-mass system with spring constant 200 N/m oscillating with amplitude 0.1 m?
questions.explanation: Total energy E = ½kA² = ½(200)(0.1)² = ½(200)(0.01) = 1 J. In the absence of friction, this energy remains constant throughout the oscillation, converting between kinetic and potential energy.

questions.question: Two identical springs (k₁ = k₂ = k) are connected in series and support a mass m. What is the effective spring constant?
questions.explanation: For springs in series, 1/k_eff = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ = 1/k + 1/k = 2/k, so k_eff = k/2. Springs in series are easier to stretch (lower effective spring constant) than a single spring.

questions.question: A horizontal spring-mass system oscillates on a frictionless surface. If the same system were oriented vertically, how would the period compare?
questions.explanation: The period T = 2π√(m/k) is independent of gravity and orientation. In the vertical case, gravity only shifts the equilibrium position but doesn't change the period. The restoring force still follows Hooke's law around the new equilibrium.
